tier1.mhms_en_title: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates
tier1.nas_treatment: Transactions translated at official CBU rate; functional currency concept not applied
tier1.mhms_treatment: Requires functional currency determination and consistent translation methodology

key_gaps.title: Functional Currency Not Formally Determined
detection_rules: Rule 1: Check the accounting policy note for an explicit statement of the entity's functional currency and the basis for that determination -- statements that simply present in UZS/USD without ever identifying or justifying a functional currency are a red flag.

Rule 2: If the entity's sales prices, labor, and major input costs are predominantly denominated/settled in a currency different from the presentation currency, check whether that mismatch was considered in determining the functional currency.

Rule 3: For a subsidiary or branch of a foreign parent, check whether the functional currency assessment considered the degree of autonomy from the parent (per the additional indicators), not just defaulted to the parent's currency.
Rule 4: Confirm the functional currency has not been changed period to period without an actual change in the underlying transactions, events, or conditions that determine it.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to formally determine the functional currency by first assessing the currency that most influences sales prices and costs of goods/services (the primary indicators), and only if that's inconclusive, the secondary financing/operating-receipts indicators -- then translate foreign currency transactions and apply this basis consistently going forward.
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company sells primarily in USD-denominated export contracts and pays most of its raw material suppliers in USD, but prepares and presents its financial statements in UZS without ever assessing or disclosing what its functional currency actually is.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: Functional currency is the currency of the primary economic environment in which the entity operates (§8) -- normally the environment in which it primarily generates and expends cash. In determining it, an entity first considers the currency that most influences the sales prices of its goods and services and the currency of the country whose competitive forces/regulations mainly determine those prices, and the currency that mainly influences labor, material, and other costs (§9); if these are not conclusive, secondary indicators (financing currency, currency in which receipts from operating activities are usually retained) are also considered (§10). Once determined, the functional currency is not changed unless there is a change in the underlying transactions, events, and conditions (§13).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #60, §8-13 (21-son BHXS "Valyuta kurslaridagi o'zgarishlarning ta'sirlari")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IAS 21.8 (Definition), IAS 21.9-13 (Determining the functional currency)

key_gaps.title: Monetary vs Non-Monetary Items Not Translated Using the Correct Basis
detection_rules: Rule 1: Check that monetary items denominated in foreign currency (cash, receivables, payables, loans) are retranslated at the closing rate at each reporting date, not left at the original transaction-date rate.

Rule 2: Check that non-monetary items measured at historical cost in a foreign currency (most inventory, PP&E, prepayments) are NOT retranslated at the closing rate -- they should stay at the exchange rate on the original transaction date.

Rule 3: Check that non-monetary items measured at fair value in a foreign currency are translated using the exchange rate at the date the fair value was determined, not the transaction date or closing rate.

Rule 4: For items like inventory carried at the lower of cost and net realizable value, confirm both the cost and NRV were translated using their own respective correct rates before comparing, rather than translating the already-compared functional-currency amount.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to classify each foreign-currency-denominated balance as monetary or non-monetary, then apply the matching translation basis: monetary items at the closing rate every period-end, non-monetary items at historical cost at the original transaction-date rate, and non-monetary items at fair value at the rate on the fair-value measurement date.
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company retranslates its USD-denominated prepaid rent (a non-monetary item carried at historical cost) at the year-end closing rate along with its USD cash and receivables, recognizing an FX gain/loss on the prepayment that IAS 21 does not permit.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: A monetary item's essential feature is a right to receive (or obligation to deliver) a fixed or determinable number of units of currency (§16) -- examples include cash, receivables, payables, and lease liabilities. Non-monetary items (prepayments, goodwill, intangible assets, inventories, PP&E, right-of-use assets) lack that feature. At each reporting date: foreign currency monetary items are translated using the closing rate; non-monetary items measured at historical cost in a foreign currency are translated using the exchange rate at the date of the transaction; and non-monetary items measured at fair value in a foreign currency are translated using the exchange rate at the date the fair value was determined (§23).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #60, §16, §23 (21-son BHXS "Valyuta kurslaridagi o'zgarishlarning ta'sirlari")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IAS 21.16 (Monetary vs non-monetary items), IAS 21.23 (Reporting at the end of subsequent periods)

key_gaps.title: Foreign Exchange Gains/Losses Not Recognized or Presented Correctly
detection_rules: Rule 1: Check that exchange differences arising on settling monetary items, or on translating monetary items at a rate different from the rate used at initial recognition or the prior reporting date, are recognized in profit or loss in the period they arise -- not deferred, capitalized, or taken directly to equity (outside the narrow net-investment-hedge exception).

Rule 2: For monetary items settled in a later period than they arose, check that the exchange difference for EACH intervening reporting period was recognized in that period, not all deferred to the settlement date.

Rule 3: Where a non-monetary item's own gain or loss is recognized in other comprehensive income (e.g., a revaluation surplus), confirm the FX component of that gain/loss is also recognized in OCI, not misclassified into profit or loss (and vice versa for items recognized in profit or loss).
Rule 4: Check that the notes disclose the amount of net exchange differences recognized in profit or loss for the period, as required for transparency.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to recognize exchange differences on monetary items in profit or loss in the period they arise (splitting the difference across each reporting period a balance remains unsettled), and match the FX component of a non-monetary item's gain or loss to wherever that item's own gain or loss is recognized (profit or loss, or OCI).
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company holds a USD-denominated loan outstanding across two reporting periods and only recognizes the cumulative exchange difference in the period the loan is finally repaid, instead of recognizing the portion attributable to each period as it arises.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: Exchange differences arising on the settlement of monetary items, or on translating monetary items at rates different from those used on initial recognition or in a previous financial statement, must be recognized in profit or loss in the period in which they arise, except for the limited net-investment-hedge case (§28). Where a monetary item arises from a foreign currency transaction and there is a change in exchange rate between the transaction date and the settlement date, an exchange difference results; if settlement occurs in a later reporting period, the exchange difference recognized in each intervening period is determined by the change in rates during that period (§29). Where a non-monetary item's gain or loss is recognized in other comprehensive income, the exchange component of that gain or loss is also recognized in other comprehensive income (§30).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #60, §28-30 (21-son BHXS "Valyuta kurslaridagi o'zgarishlarning ta'sirlari")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IAS 21.28 (Recognition of exchange differences), IAS 21.29-30 (Settlement in a later period; OCI-linked items)

tier2.nas_treatment: Consolidation based on ownership percentage thresholds
tier2.mhms_treatment: Requires control-based consolidation assessment (power, exposure, ability to affect returns)

key_gaps.title: Consolidation Based on Ownership Percentage Instead of a Control Assessment
detection_rules: Rule 1: Check whether entities were consolidated (or excluded from consolidation) purely based on crossing an ownership percentage threshold (e.g. >50%), with no documented assessment of power, exposure to variable returns, and the ability to use that power.

Rule 2: Look for an investee where the reporting entity holds less than 50% of voting rights but has other rights (e.g. contractual management rights, potential voting rights, a dominant minority position with other shareholders dispersed) that could still give it control -- if such an investee is NOT consolidated, check whether control was properly assessed rather than assumed absent based on the ownership percentage alone.

Rule 3: Conversely, check whether an investee where the entity holds a majority stake but lacks practical power (e.g. governance rights held by another party, protective rights only) has been consolidated anyway just because of the ownership percentage.
Rule 4: Confirm control was reassessed when facts and circumstances changed (e.g. changes in voting rights, contractual arrangements), not left as a one-time determination at acquisition.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to assess control for each investee using the three-part test -- power over the investee, exposure or rights to variable returns from it, and the ability to use that power to affect the amount of those returns -- rather than relying on an ownership percentage threshold alone, and consolidate (or deconsolidate) based on that assessment.
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company holds 45% of the voting shares in another entity, with the remaining 55% dispersed among many small unrelated shareholders who rarely vote as a bloc, giving the 45% holder practical power to direct the investee's relevant activities -- but the investee is not consolidated because the ownership stake is below the 50% threshold, without any documented control assessment.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: An investor must determine whether it is a parent by assessing whether it controls the investee, regardless of the nature of its involvement (§5). An investor controls an investee only if it has ALL of: power over the investee, exposure or rights to variable returns from its involvement with the investee, and the ability to use its power over the investee to affect the amount of the investor's returns (§6-7). The investor must consider all facts and circumstances in assessing control, and must reassess whether it controls an investee if facts and circumstances indicate that one or more of the three elements of control have changed (§8).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #12, §5-8 (10-son MHXS "Konsolidatsiyalashgan moliyaviy hisobot")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IFRS 10.5 (Determining parent status), IFRS 10.6-7 (Definition of control), IFRS 10.8 (Reassessment)

key_gaps.title: Non-Controlling Interest Not Separately Presented or Allocated Loss-Sharing Ignored
detection_rules: Rule 1: Check that non-controlling interests are presented within equity in the consolidated balance sheet, separately from the equity attributable to the parent's owners, rather than being shown as a liability or netted against the parent's equity.

Rule 2: Check that profit or loss and each component of other comprehensive income are allocated between the parent and non-controlling interest owners based on their respective ownership, even in periods where the subsidiary made a loss (which can push NCI's balance negative).

Rule 3: Confirm total comprehensive income is attributed to the parent and NCI even when this results in a deficit (negative) balance for the non-controlling interest, rather than allocating all losses to the parent alone.

Rule 4: If a partial disposal or acquisition of additional shares in a subsidiary occurred without a change in control, check that this was accounted for as an equity transaction (an adjustment between NCI and parent equity), not as a gain or loss in profit or loss.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to present non-controlling interests as a separate component within consolidated equity (not as a liability), allocate profit/loss and OCI between the parent and NCI based on their ownership even where this produces a negative NCI balance, and account for any change in ownership interest that does not result in a loss of control as a transaction with owners in their capacity as owners (an equity adjustment, not a gain/loss).
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A subsidiary that is 70% owned made a significant loss for the year, and the consolidated financial statements allocate the entire loss to the parent's equity, leaving the non-controlling interest balance unchanged, instead of allocating 30% of the loss to NCI (even if that produces a negative NCI balance).
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: A parent must present non-controlling interests in the consolidated statement of financial position within equity, separately from the equity of the owners of the parent (§22). Changes in a parent's ownership interest in a subsidiary that do not result in a loss of control are accounted for as equity transactions -- transactions with owners in their capacity as owners (§23). Profit or loss and each component of other comprehensive income are attributed to the owners of the parent and to the non-controlling interests -- total comprehensive income is attributed to the parent and NCI even if this results in the non-controlling interests having a deficit balance.
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #12, §22-23, B94 (10-son MHXS "Konsolidatsiyalashgan moliyaviy hisobot")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IFRS 10.22 (NCI presented within equity), IFRS 10.23 (Ownership changes without loss of control), IFRS 10.B94 (Allocation of profit/loss and OCI to NCI)

key_gaps.title: Intragroup Balances and Transactions Not Fully Eliminated on Consolidation
detection_rules: Rule 1: Check that the parent's investment balance in each subsidiary is eliminated against the parent's share of that subsidiary's equity, rather than both being left on the consolidated balance sheet.

Rule 2: Check that intragroup assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses, and cash flows relating to transactions between group entities are fully eliminated -- e.g. an intercompany receivable/payable pair, or intercompany sales and purchases, should net to zero on consolidation.

Rule 3: For inventory or PP&E still held within the group that was transferred between group entities at a markup, check whether the unrealized profit embedded in that asset's carrying amount was eliminated, not left recognized as if it were a sale to an external party.

Rule 4: Where intragroup losses may indicate impairment of the underlying asset, confirm that impairment is still recognized in the consolidated financial statements even though the intragroup loss itself is eliminated.

Rule 5: Check that group members used consistent accounting policies for similar transactions when preparing the consolidated financial statements, with adjustments made to any group member's financial statements prepared using a different policy.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to eliminate the parent's investment in each subsidiary against the parent's share of that subsidiary's equity, fully eliminate intragroup assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows arising from transactions between group entities (including any unrealized profit in year-end inventory or PP&E transferred within the group), while still recognizing any impairment that an intragroup loss may point to.
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A parent sells inventory to its subsidiary at a markup, and at year-end the subsidiary still holds that inventory unsold to an external party -- the consolidated financial statements still include the intercompany profit embedded in that inventory's carrying amount because the intragroup sale and the resulting unrealized profit were never eliminated.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: In preparing consolidated financial statements: the assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses, and cash flows of the parent are combined with those of its subsidiaries line by line; the carrying amount of the parent's investment in each subsidiary is eliminated (offset) against the parent's share of equity in each subsidiary; and intragroup assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses, and cash flows relating to transactions between group entities are eliminated in full -- profits or losses from intragroup transactions recognized in assets such as inventory and PP&E are eliminated in full, though intragroup losses may indicate an impairment that must still be recognized in the consolidated financial statements (§B86). Uniform accounting policies must be applied across the group, with adjustments made to a group member's financial statements if it uses different policies for similar transactions (§B87).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #12, §B86-B87 (10-son MHXS "Konsolidatsiyalashgan moliyaviy hisobot")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IFRS 10.B86 (Consolidation procedures: combination, investment elimination, intragroup elimination), IFRS 10.B87 (Uniform accounting policies)

tier2.mhms_uz_title: Zahiralar, shartli majburiyatlar va shartli aktivlar
tier2.mhms_en_title: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
tier2.nas_treatment: Provisions recognized mainly per statutory/tax rules
tier2.mhms_treatment: Requires present-obligation, probable-outflow, and reliable-estimate recognition test

key_gaps.title: Provisions Recognized Without Testing the Three Recognition Criteria
detection_rules: Rule 1: Check whether recognized provisions correspond to a present obligation (legal or constructive) arising from a past event, rather than being set up for possible future operating costs or management's general intention to spend.

Rule 2: For provisions based on a constructive obligation (no contract or law requiring payment), check whether the entity's past practice, published policy, or specific current statement actually created a valid expectation in other parties that it would discharge that responsibility -- absent that, a constructive obligation does not exist.
Rule 3: Confirm each recognized provision has an outflow of resources assessed as probable (more likely than not), not merely possible.

Rule 4: Check that provisions are only recognized where the obligation amount can be reliably estimated -- if not, confirm it was disclosed as a contingent liability instead of recognized as a provision.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to test each recognized provision against all three criteria -- a present legal or constructive obligation from a past event, a probable (not merely possible) outflow of resources, and a reliable estimate of the amount -- and derecognize any provision that fails one of these, reclassifying it as a contingent liability disclosure if appropriate instead.
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company recognizes a provision for anticipated future restructuring costs based only on management's internal intention to restructure next year, with no detailed formal plan announced to any affected parties -- this fails the present-obligation criterion since no past event has created an actual obligation yet.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: A provision is recognized only when: the entity has a present obligation (legal or constructive) as a result of a past event; it is probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation; and a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation (§14). If these conditions are not met, no provision is recognized. A constructive obligation arises from an entity's actions where, through an established pattern of past practice, published policies, or a sufficiently specific current statement, the entity has indicated to other parties that it will accept certain responsibilities, and has created a valid expectation on the part of those other parties that it will discharge those responsibilities (§10).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #35, §10, §14 (37-son BHXS "Baholangan majburiyatlar, shartli majburiyatlar va shartli aktivlar")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IAS 37.10 (Definitions), IAS 37.14 (Recognition criteria)

key_gaps.title: Contingent Liabilities Not Disclosed
detection_rules: Rule 1: Look for pending legal claims, guarantees given, or disputed tax assessments mentioned anywhere in management commentary or minutes that are not reflected as either a provision or a contingent liability disclosure in the notes.

Rule 2: For a possible obligation whose existence will be confirmed only by an uncertain future event outside the entity's control, confirm it is disclosed as a contingent liability rather than silently omitted.

Rule 3: For a present obligation that is not recognized because outflow is not probable, or the amount can't be reliably estimated, check that it is still disclosed as a contingent liability (unless the probability of outflow is remote).

Rule 4: Check that contingent liability disclosures include a brief description of its nature and, where practicable, an estimate of its financial effect, an indication of uncertainties around amount/timing, and the possibility of any reimbursement.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to identify possible obligations that depend on uncertain future events, and present obligations that fail the probable-outflow or reliable-estimate recognition tests, and disclose each as a contingent liability (nature, estimated financial effect where practicable, and related uncertainties) unless the chance of any outflow is remote.
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company is a defendant in an ongoing lawsuit with a reasonably possible (but not probable) chance of an adverse outcome, and the financial statements make no mention of this at all -- omitting the contingent liability disclosure required even though no provision is recognized.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: Unless the possibility of any outflow of resources is remote, an entity must disclose, for each class of contingent liability at the reporting date, a brief description of its nature and, where practicable: an estimate of its financial effect, an indication of the uncertainties relating to the amount or timing of any outflow, and the possibility of any reimbursement (§86). Items forming a class must be sufficiently similar in nature for this purpose (§87). Where a provision and a contingent liability arise from the same set of circumstances, the entity discloses the link between them (§88).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #35, §86-88 (37-son BHXS "Baholangan majburiyatlar, shartli majburiyatlar va shartli aktivlar")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IAS 37.86 (Contingent liability disclosure requirements), IAS 37.87-88 (Classes and linkage to provisions)

key_gaps.title: Long-Term Provisions Not Discounted to Present Value
detection_rules: Rule 1: For provisions expected to be settled more than approximately a year in the future (e.g. long-term decommissioning, warranty, or legal provisions), check whether the recognized amount reflects the present value of expected settlement cash flows rather than the undiscounted nominal expected cost.

Rule 2: Where discounting was applied, check that the discount rate used is a pre-tax rate reflecting current market assessments of the time value of money and risks specific to the liability, not a general corporate cost-of-capital rate that also embeds unrelated risk adjustments.
Rule 3: Confirm the discount rate does not double-count risk that has already been reflected as an adjustment to the estimated future cash flows themselves.
Rule 4: Check that the unwinding of the discount (the increase in a provision's carrying amount as time passes) is recognized as a finance cost, not folded into the operating provision expense.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to discount the expenditures expected to be required to settle any provision where the time value of money is material, using a pre-tax discount rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the liability, and recognize the periodic unwinding of that discount as a finance cost.
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company recognizes a decommissioning provision for a facility expected to be dismantled in 15 years at its full undiscounted future cost, rather than at the present value of that future cash outflow, materially overstating the liability today.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: Where the effect of the time value of money is material, the amount of a provision must be the present value of the expenditures expected to be required to settle the obligation (§45). Because of the time value of money, provisions relating to cash outflows that arise soon after the reporting date are more onerous than those where cash outflows of the same amount arise later -- provisions are discounted, where the effect is material (§46). The discount rate(s) must be a pre-tax rate (or rates) that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the liability -- the discount rate(s) must not reflect risks for which future cash flow estimates have already been adjusted (§47).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #35, §45-47 (37-son BHXS "Baholangan majburiyatlar, shartli majburiyatlar va shartli aktivlar")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IAS 37.45 (Present value measurement), IAS 37.46 (Materiality of discounting), IAS 37.47 (Discount rate)

tier2.nas_treatment: Short-term benefits and statutory obligations accrued; no actuarial valuation
tier2.mhms_treatment: Requires actuarial valuation for post-employment/long-term defined benefit obligations

key_gaps.title: Unused Accumulating Leave/Vacation Entitlement Not Accrued
detection_rules: Rule 1: Check whether the entity accrues a liability for employees' unused, carried-forward vacation/leave entitlement at each reporting date, rather than only expensing leave when it is actually taken.

Rule 2: Confirm the accrual is measured as the additional amount the entity expects to pay as a result of the unused accumulated entitlement at period end (extra leave days x pay rate), not just a notional or zero balance.

Rule 3: Check whether the accrual is recognized even for non-vesting accumulating leave (employees not entitled to a cash payment for unused leave on termination) -- a liability still arises because employees render service that increases their entitlement, regardless of whether it's ultimately paid out in cash or taken as time off.
Rule 4: Confirm the amount reflects that some employees may leave before using their carried-forward entitlement, where that affects the obligation's measurement.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to recognize a liability at each reporting date for the additional amount expected to be paid or utilized as a result of employees' unused accumulated leave entitlement carried forward from the period, rather than expensing leave only when it is taken.
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company's 100 employees each accrue paid annual leave that can be carried forward one year, and a significant number have unused leave balances at year-end, but the company only recognizes leave expense as employees actually take time off, with no year-end accrual for the carried-forward entitlement.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: An entity recognizes the expected cost of short-term employee benefits in the form of compensated absences when the employee renders service that increases their entitlement to future compensated absences, in the case of accumulating compensated absences (§13). Accumulating compensated absences are those that are carried forward and can be used in future periods if the current period's entitlement is not used in full -- these may be vesting (employees entitled to a cash payment for unused entitlement on leaving) or non-vesting. An obligation arises as employees render service that increases their entitlement, and is recognized even if non-vesting, though the possibility employees may leave before using a non-vesting entitlement affects the measurement of that obligation (§15). The entity measures the expected cost of accumulating compensated absences as the additional amount it expects to pay as a result of the unused entitlement accumulated at the reporting date (§16).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #42, §13, §15-16 (19-son BHXS "Xodimlarning daromadlari")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IAS 19.13 (Recognition of short-term compensated absences), IAS 19.15-16 (Accumulating compensated absences measurement)

key_gaps.title: Long-Term Employee Benefit Obligations Not Actuarially Valued
detection_rules: Rule 1: Look for long-service/jubilee awards, long-term disability benefits, or deferred compensation payable more than 12 months after the period in which employees render the related service -- check whether these are measured using an actuarial method, or simply accrued at face/nominal value.

Rule 2: For any such long-term benefit obligation, confirm it was measured using the Projected Unit Credit Method (the same actuarial approach used for defined benefit pension obligations), incorporating demographic assumptions (employee turnover, mortality) and financial assumptions (future salary increases).

Rule 3: Check that the net obligation recognized in profit or loss includes current service cost and net interest on the net obligation, consistent with how post-employment defined benefit obligations are measured.

Rule 4: Confirm that no long-term employee benefit obligation was left completely unrecognized just because its ultimate settlement is uncertain in timing or amount -- uncertainty is addressed through actuarial estimation, not omission.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to identify employee benefits payable more than twelve months after the period in which the related service was rendered (long-service awards, long-term disability benefits, deferred bonuses) and measure the resulting obligation using an actuarial method (the same projected unit credit approach used for defined benefit pension plans) rather than a simple undiscounted accrual.
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company promises a lump-sum jubilee bonus to employees who complete 20 years of service, but records no liability for this obligation at all until the bonus is actually paid, instead of building up an actuarially estimated obligation as employees render the qualifying service.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: Other long-term employee benefits include items such as long-term paid absences (e.g. long-service or sabbatical leave), jubilee or other long-service benefits, long-term disability benefits, profit-sharing and bonuses payable more than twelve months after the end of the period in which employees render the related service, and deferred compensation (§153). Because the measurement of other long-term employee benefits is not usually subject to the same degree of uncertainty as post-employment benefits, the standard requires a simplified method of accounting for them, applying the same recognition and measurement approach (§56-98, §113-115) used for defined benefit post-employment plans, but without recognizing remeasurements in other comprehensive income (§154-155). The net total of current service cost, net interest on the net obligation, and remeasurements of the net obligation is recognized in profit or loss (§156).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #42, §57, §153, §155-156 (19-son BHXS "Xodimlarning daromadlari")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IAS 19.57 (Projected unit credit method), IAS 19.153 (Other long-term benefits defined), IAS 19.155-156 (Simplified recognition and measurement)

tier2.nas_treatment: Charter capital recorded at registered/statutory value
tier2.mhms_treatment: Requires classification between liability and equity components for compound instruments

key_gaps.title: Compound Financial Instruments Not Split into Liability and Equity Components
detection_rules: Rule 1: Look for any issued instrument with both a debt-like feature (fixed repayment/interest obligation) AND an equity-like feature (e.g. an option for the holder to convert into a fixed number of the entity's own shares) -- check whether it was split into separate liability and equity components rather than recorded entirely as a single liability.

Rule 2: Confirm the liability component was measured first, at the fair value of a similar liability without the conversion feature, with the equity component recognized as the residual (total instrument fair value less the liability component) -- not the other way around.
Rule 3: Check that no gain or loss was recognized on initial recognition from splitting the instrument into its two components.

Rule 4: Confirm the classification of the debt and equity components was not reassessed later just because conversion became more or less likely -- the original split stands until actual conversion, redemption, or another transaction changes it.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to split any issued compound instrument (e.g. a convertible bond) into a financial liability component and an equity component at issuance, measuring the liability first at the fair value of a similar instrument without the conversion feature, and recognizing the equity component as the residual amount, with no gain or loss on the split itself.
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company issues a bond convertible into a fixed number of its own ordinary shares and records the entire proceeds as a single financial liability, without separating out the value of the conversion option as a component of equity.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: The issuer of a non-derivative financial instrument must evaluate the terms of the instrument to determine whether it contains both a liability and an equity component, and classify each component separately as a financial liability, financial asset, or equity instrument (§28). A bond or similar instrument convertible by the holder into a fixed number of the entity's ordinary shares is a compound financial instrument comprising a financial liability (a contractual arrangement to deliver cash or another financial asset) and an equity instrument (a call option granting the holder the right to convert into a fixed number of ordinary shares) (§29). The liability component is measured first at the fair value of a similar liability without an equity conversion option; the equity component is recognized as the residual, being the fair value of the compound instrument as a whole less the fair value of the liability component separately determined, with no gain or loss arising from the split (§31-32).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #45, §28-32 (32-son BHXS "Moliyaviy instrumentlar: taqdim etish")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IAS 32.28-29 (Compound instrument classification), IAS 32.31-32 (Split measurement approach)

key_gaps.title: Treasury Shares Not Deducted from Equity or Disclosed
detection_rules: Rule 1: Check whether repurchased own equity instruments (treasury shares) are deducted directly from equity, rather than shown as a financial asset or investment on the balance sheet.

Rule 2: Confirm no gain or loss was recognized in profit or loss on the purchase, sale, issuance, or cancellation of the entity's own equity instruments -- consideration paid or received should be recognized directly in equity.
Rule 3: Check that the notes or a separate statement of financial position disclose the amount of treasury shares held, as required, and not simply netted away with no visibility.
Rule 4: If treasury shares were acquired from a related party, confirm the related-party disclosure requirements were also applied.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: You will need to deduct any repurchased own equity instruments (treasury shares) directly from equity rather than recognizing them as an asset, recognize no gain or loss on their purchase/sale/reissue/cancellation (with consideration paid or received recognized directly in equity), and disclose the amount held.
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company buys back some of its own shares on the market and records them as a financial asset investment at cost, later recognizing a gain in profit or loss when it resells them at a higher price -- treasury shares should instead have been deducted from equity with no gain or loss recognized on the transaction.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: If an entity reacquires its own equity instruments, those instruments ("treasury shares") must be deducted from equity. No gain or loss is recognized in profit or loss on the purchase, sale, issue, or cancellation of an entity's own equity instruments. Such treasury shares may be held by the entity or by other members of the consolidated group. Consideration paid or received is recognized directly in equity (§33). The amount of treasury shares held must be disclosed separately either on the face of the statement of financial position or in the notes, in accordance with IAS 1; if treasury shares are acquired from related parties, related-party disclosure requirements also apply (§34).
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #45, §33-34 (32-son BHXS "Moliyaviy instrumentlar: taqdim etish")
key_gaps.ifrs_ref: IAS 32.33 (Treasury shares deducted from equity, no gain/loss), IAS 32.34 (Disclosure requirement)

tier2.nas_treatment: Current tax expense recognized per tax return; limited deferred tax recognition
tier2.mhms_treatment: Requires comprehensive deferred tax recognition via balance sheet temporary differences

key_gaps.title: Income Tax - Deferred Tax Assets and Liabilities
detection_rules: Rule 1: Check for any deferred tax asset/liability line; complete absence, with only a 'current tax payable' line, signals deferred tax was not recognized.
Rule 2: For assets with book vs. tax depreciation rate differences, verify whether the resulting temporary difference was quantified and deferred tax recognized.
Rule 3: Check for unused tax losses carried forward with no corresponding deferred tax asset, or recognized without assessing probable future taxable profit.
Rule 4: Look for PP&E revaluation (Gap 22.1) without corresponding deferred tax on the revaluation surplus.
key_gaps.adjustment_hint: Compare the tax base of each material asset/liability against its book carrying amount, identify resulting temporary differences, and recognize the corresponding deferred tax liabilities/assets (assets only to the extent future taxable profit is probable). This affects both the balance sheet (new DTA/DTL lines) and income statement (deferred tax expense/income).
key_gaps.example: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A company's equipment has a book value of 100,000,000 UZS but a tax base of 70,000,000 UZS due to faster tax depreciation, with no deferred tax recognized. Under IAS 12.5 and .7-8, this 30,000,000 UZS taxable temporary difference requires a deferred tax liability at the applicable tax rate.
key_gaps.mhms_treatment: A deferred tax liability or asset arises whenever the carrying amount of an asset or liability differs from its tax base, creating a 'temporary difference.' The tax base of an asset is the amount deductible for tax purposes against taxable economic benefits when the entity recovers the carrying amount; if benefits are not taxable, tax base equals carrying amount. The tax base of a liability is generally its carrying amount less amounts deductible in future periods. Taxable temporary differences give rise to deferred tax liabilities; deductible temporary differences give rise to deferred tax assets. Deferred tax must generally be recognized for essentially all temporary differences - not just the current-period tax liability from the tax return. A deferred tax asset is also recognized for unused tax losses/credits carried forward, to the extent future taxable profit is probable.
key_gaps.lex_uz_ref: Lex.uz MHMS #55, §5 (ta'riflar), §7-8 (12-son BHXS "Foyda soliqlari")
